claims.assertion: This was a RydeTAXI trip (metered, $41.17 total), so the fare varies with distance and the detour kilometres were billed to the rider.
The GPS track shows the trip was 19.2 km against a 15.5 km optimal route, i.e. 3.8 km (+24%) more than the shortest direct route.
There is one off-route segment 17:37–17:50 in which 5.85 km was driven where the optimal route covers 2.68 km, adding 3.17 km and reaching up to 1172 m from the optimal route.

The rider named no location and the driver's own statement says he chose the 7-Eleven 'I know' and went there; the GPS shows the actual stop at 17:41–17:45 was 5306 m from the pickup and 4755 m from the drop-off, i.e. the driver's unilateral choice took the trip 1172 m off the optimal route — so the segment's extra kilometres are not exempted by the rider's stop request.
The stop agreement came at 17:33, before the off-route segment began at 17:37, but what was agreed was only a 2-minute stop, not the 5.85 km route change the driver actually made.

No traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window and the only speed bands on PIE and CTE were band 4 (30–39 km/h), so the driver has no traffic-based 'reasonable cause' for the off-route segment under RD-4.
As the off-route segment is unexempted, the refund is the extra kilometres at the trip's per-km rate: 3.17 km × $1.41/km = $4.47, rounded to the cent (the fare confirms the $1.41/km distance rate).

Within that same segment the driver was stationary 4 min 10 s at 17:41–17:45 at a spot 5306 m from pickup, billed as a $1.08 waiting fee (4.2 min × $0.26/min); under RD-3(c) RydeTAXI waiting time is charged at the meter, so we do not dispute this $1.08 and confine the claim to the 3.17 km.
The driver's account has 0 upheld disputes in 90 d, so no flag_account is requested; the breach is single, not repeated.

weaknesses: The rider did ask for a 7-Eleven stop and the driver agreed (F9, F10), so the driver will argue the whole detour is a passenger-requested stop and therefore exempt under RD-3; our case turns on the rider naming no location and the app stop being 5306 m from pickup and 1172 m off-route (F2, F4, F11), which is a finer distinction than a bare 'you consented' reading.

The trip ran 33.4 min vs 22 min estimated (F3) while PIE and CTE were only band 4, i.e. 30–39 km/h — the driver may use these traffic facts (F12, F13) to portray slow expressway conditions as the cause of the extra distance, though F14 records no incident and band 4 is not band 1–2 congestion.
The rider has 4 disputes in the last 90 d, 2 upheld, none route-related (F16); the driver can point to this pattern to suggest a frequent-dispute rider.

The detour is 3.17 km under our reading, but excess distance billed is 3.8 km (F5) — the 0.63 km residual is not claimed, so on any map-matching error in the 0.2 km noise band our recoverable amount is small in absolute terms.

claims.assertion: The 4 min 10 s stop at 17:41–17:45 was a rider-requested stop (she asked at 17:33 for a 7-Eleven and the driver accepted at 17:33), so the stop itself must not be treated as an unexplained deviation; only the route taken to it is under review.

That request did not name a location, and the driver chose a store that sits off the optimal route; GPS shows the detour segment reached up to 1172 m from the optimal route, so the driver could not have been following the named route when he selected the store.

No pre-departure agreement covers the store choice: the rider's only message is the unnamed 7-Eleven request at 17:33, and the detour segment with extra km begins at 17:37, so consent in the sense of 'mutual agreement before you go' for this specific location is absent.

No reasonable-cause exemption is available: the sole traffic records are PIE and CE speed band 4 (30–39 km/h), and band 4 is nowhere near the band 1–2 (severe congestion) threshold that could corroborate a congestion reroute (and band 2 alone is not sufficient), while no traffic incidents at all were recorded near the route.

The only off-route segment runs 17:37–17:50 and added 3.17 km; because this is RydeTAXI (metered), the refund should be capped at the metered value of that one unexempted segment, not the whole excess.

Applying the RD-2 per-km rate implied by this trip ($27.11 distance fare ÷ 19.2 km = $1.41/km) to the 3.17 km unexempted detour segment yields a mileage refund of $4.47, and per RD-2 the ≤0.25 km map-matching residual (here 3.8 km excess billed vs 3.17 km segment = 0.63 km, of which the non-segment remainder is not refundable in RydeTAXI anyway) must not be added.

The 4.2 min in-trip stop is chargeable as metered waiting time for RydeTAXI, and the $1.08 waiting line matches that meter unit, so it should stand; but the billed excess-distance line should be reduced to the metered value of the unexempted segment only.
The driver has no upheld route dispute in the last 90 days (1 dispute filed, 0 upheld, route 0), so the 'repeated' threshold for flag_account is not met even though a refund is now owed.

weaknesses: The system records contradict the driver's own statement: F11 says 'I went to the one I know', and F4 shows a 5.85 km detour reaching 1172 m off the optimal route, so the rider's account that she asked for a stop 'on the way' (F9) is corroborated by the GPS and the stop was not on the optimal route.

The rider named no location (F9), and there is no message showing the driver told her which store or how far off it was before leaving the optimal route, so RD-3(b) and RD-5 defeat any claim that the rider's 'stop on the way' consent covered a 3.17 km off-route excursion.

There is no traffic excuse to fall back on: F14 shows no incidents on the optimal route, and F12/F13 show only band 4 (30–39 km/h), below the band 1–2 congestion bands of RD-4(b) — and F15 shows fair weather, so weather cannot justify the reroute either.

The trip-wide excess (3.8 km vs 3.17 km in-segment, F1/F4) leaves roughly 0.63 km of billed excess the driver cannot explain; although RD-2 excludes that residual from this refund, the judge may read the unexplained remainder as evidence of further route slippage.

events.body:
This is a completed RydeTAXI trip, charged on the meter ($41.17 with distance $27.11 over 19.2 km) [F8], so distance feeds the fare and detour kilometres are billed to the rider; the per-km rate is $27.11 ÷ 19.2 km = $1.4098/km [F8][RD-2]. GPS shows 19.2 km actual against a 15.5 km optimal route, +3.8 km, and one off-route segment 17:37–17:50 (5.85 km where the optimal route covers 2.68 km), adding 3.17 km and reaching up to 1172 m off route [F1][F4][RD-1].

That single segment is not exempted. The rider's only message was "Can you stop at a 7-Eleven on the way? Just need 2 minutes" at 17:33, and the driver replied only "Ok" [F9][F10]; the rider named no location, and the driver's own statement says he went to "the one I know" [F11]. The stop itself, at 17:41–17:45, was 5306 m from the pickup and 4755 m from the drop-off [F2]. Because the rider named no place and the driver unilaterally chose a location well off the optimal route without previously naming it, the segment's extra kilometres are not exempted by the stop request [F2][F4][F9][F11][RD-3].

No consent exemption applies: the 17:33 agreement preceded the 17:37 segment start, but what was agreed was a two-minute stop, not a 5.85 km route change, and no message shows the driver named the store or its corridor before leaving the optimal route [F4][F9][F10][RD-5]. No reasonable-cause exemption applies either: no traffic incident was recorded near the route [F14], the only speed records are PIE and CTE band 4 (30–39 km/h), which is not band 1–2 and in any case is only corroborative [F12][F13][RD-4]. Weather was fair [F15].

The refund is therefore the extra kilometres of the one unexempted segment at the trip's own per-km rate: 3.17 km × ($27.11 ÷ 19.2 km = $1.4098/km) = $4.47 [F4][F8][RD-2]. No account flag attaches. RD-6 requires a refund > 0 (met here) plus a prior upheld route dispute in 90 days; the driver's profile shows 1 dispute, 0 upheld, route 0 [F17][RD-6].
